name: Jagua tattoos

card.summary: A plant-based temporary body stain made from genipin in unripe jagua fruit that darkens on skin to a blue-black design, used for tattoo-style body art without needles.
card.aka: Genipa americana; genipap; huito; jenipapo; jagua henna
card.note: Contact allergy to genipin has been reported in case reports, including severe reactions.

quick.overview:
Jagua tattoos are temporary designs painted onto the skin with a gel or juice from the unripe fruit of the jagua tree (Genipa americana). The stain turns blue-black over several hours, giving the look of a tattoo or dark henna without needles or permanent ink.

People use it for body art, event looks and trying out a tattoo design. The colouring comes from genipin, a compound in the fruit that reacts with proteins in the outer skin. Published research is mostly case reports of allergic reactions and lab analyses of commercial products.
quick.how: Artists or kits apply a jagua-based gel with a stencil or a fine applicator, leave it on for a period, and then remove the gel; the colour continues to darken over the following hours. Products are sold as an alternative to black henna and fade over about one to two weeks as the skin sheds.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to genipin, in some cases severe. Laboratory analyses of commercial henna and jagua products have found that many are not labelled according to their contents, and some contain metallic impurities. People with prior reactions to temporary tattoo dyes are generally advised by dermatologists to be cautious and consider patch testing.

lead: Jagua tattoos are temporary skin designs made with an extract of the unripe fruit of Genipa americana, a tree native to tropical Central and South America known as jagua, genipap, huito or jenipapo.[1] The extract contains genipin, which reacts with skin proteins to produce a blue-black stain, so the result resembles a needle tattoo without breaking the skin.[1][2]

For appearance, people use jagua to try tattoo designs, decorate for festivals and events, or obtain a black temporary design as an alternative to black henna, which commonly contains paraphenylenediamine (PPD).[3] Jagua products were marketed as PPD-free and 'dermatologically tested', and the stain has long been used by Indigenous peoples of South America for body painting.[4]

The research literature consists mainly of dermatology case reports of allergic contact dermatitis to genipin, an overview of tattoo hypersensitivity, and chemical analyses of commercial products.[3][4][5][6] The same fruit pigment, processed into 'jagua blue', is separately evaluated as a food colour; EFSA published a safety opinion in 2025.[7]

paras: Genipa americana is a medium-sized tree of tropical Central and South America. Its unripe fruit contains genipin, which develops a blue-black colour on contact with skin proteins; the fruit has been used for body painting, insect repellent and food.[1][2]
Commercial jagua tattoo products are typically a gel made from the extract, applied through a stencil or by hand. The colour is not visible immediately and deepens over hours after application.[1]

Extracts of jagua and the related gardenia fruit have been used by Indigenous people in South America, and gardenia in traditional Chinese medicine, for centuries.[4] The plant's names in several languages, and a reconstructed word in the Proto-Tucanoan language, point to long-standing use of the dye.[8]
Jagua body art became popular in Europe and North America in the 2010s as a temporary tattoo option marketed as free of PPD, the allergen associated with black henna.[4]

No controlled trials of jagua tattoos for appearance outcomes have been published. Clinical literature is mostly case reports. A 2017 report described allergic contact dermatitis in a person who developed sensitization to genipin after a jagua tattoo, noting the product had been described as dermatologically tested.[4] Further case reports from 2017, 2019 and 2024 describe dermatitis, including a 2019 report of severe allergic dermatitis attributed to genipin.[5][6][9]

A 2020 review of tattoo hypersensitivity lists genipin contact allergy among reported reactions to temporary tattoos, next to PPD in black henna.[3] Laboratory work has analysed 34 commercial henna and jagua products and found that many are not labelled according to their content and may contain metallic impurities, and authors call for specific regulatory requirements.[10][11]

Dermatologists describe reactions mainly as allergic contact dermatitis at the application site.[3][4] Because ingredient labels on temporary tattoo products are often incomplete, researchers writing about cosmetic regulation have called for clearer controls.[10]

The food use of jagua blue (genipin reacted with glycine) was assessed by EFSA in 2025, which derived an acceptable daily intake from animal toxicity studies; this relates to ingestion, not skin application.[7]

timeline.event: Jagua blue assessed in the food-science literature as a natural blue colourant.[12]
Case reports of allergic contact dermatitis from jagua tattoos published.[4][5]
Report of severe allergic dermatitis attributed to genipin in a temporary tattoo.[6]
